claim: Many people, and particularly individuals with attention deficit (hyperactivity) disorder (AD(H)D), find it difficult to maintain attention during classroom learning.
source: Many people, and particularly individuals with attention deficit (hyperactivity) disorder (AD(H)D), find it difficult to maintain attention during classroom learning.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about ADHD and attention difficulties in classroom settings.

claim: Traditional paradigms used to evaluate attention do not capture the complexity and dynamic nature of real-life classrooms.
source: However, traditional paradigms used to evaluate attention do not capture the complexity and dynamic nature of real-life classrooms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction discussing limitations of current tools.

claim: Individuals with AD(H)D exhibited higher neural responses to irrelevant sounds relative to controls.
source: Individuals with AD(H)D exhibited higher neural responses to irrelevant sounds and reduced speech tracking of the teacher, relative to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ERP analysis showing larger N1 responses in the ADHD group.

claim: Individuals with AD(H)D exhibited reduced speech tracking of the teacher relative to controls.
source: Individuals with AD(H)D exhibited higher neural responses to irrelevant sounds and reduced speech tracking of the teacher, relative to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the decoding model showing lower reconstruction correlations in the ADHD group.

claim: The power of alpha-oscillations contributed to explaining variance in self-reported AD(H)D symptoms across the sample.
source: Additional neurophysiological measures, such the power of alpha-oscillations and frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher, contributed to explaining variance in self-reported AD(H)D symptoms across the sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate regression analysis showing alpha-power as a dominant predictor of ASRS scores.

claim: The frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher contributed to explaining variance in self-reported AD(H)D symptoms across the sample.
source: Additional neurophysiological measures, such the power of alpha-oscillations and frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher, contributed to explaining variance in self-reported AD(H)D symptoms across the sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate regression analysis showing gaze-shifts as a dominant predictor of ASRS scores.

claim: Maintaining attention in a classroom requires listening, processing, and comprehending the teacher's speech over a prolonged period of time.
source: Doing so requires listening, processing, and comprehending the teacher's speech over a prolonged period of time, while avoiding distraction from both irrelevant background sounds and internal mind-wandering (Smallwood et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2015; Esterman and Rothlein, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on attention and mind-wandering.

claim: Maintaining attention in a classroom requires avoiding distraction from irrelevant background sounds and internal mind-wandering.
source: Doing so requires listening, processing, and comprehending the teacher's speech over a prolonged period of time, while avoiding distraction from both irrelevant background sounds and internal mind-wandering (Smallwood et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2015; Esterman and Rothlein, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on attention and mind-wandering.

claim: AD(H)D is often characterized by increased proneness to distraction and mind-wandering and poorer sustained attention.
source: This task is supposedly even more difficult for individuals diagnosed with attention-deficit disorder or attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder (referred to jointly as AD(H)D), which is often characterized by increase proneness to distraction and mind-wandering and poorer sustained attention (Avisar and Shalev, 2011; Berger and Cassuto, 2014; Merrill et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ADHD characteristics.

claim: Individuals are most likely to seek clinical help as a result of attentional difficulties experienced in school contexts.
source: Unsurprisingly perhaps, individuals are most likely to seek clinical help as a result of attentional difficulties experienced in school contexts (Litner, 2003), and there is a tight link between attention performance and learning outcomes (Loe and Feldman, 2007; Gray et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Litner, 2003.

claim: There is a tight link between attention performance and learning outcomes.
source: Unsurprisingly perhaps, individuals are most likely to seek clinical help as a result of attentional difficulties experienced in school contexts (Litner, 2003), and there is a tight link between attention performance and learning outcomes (Loe and Feldman, 2007; Gray et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Loe and Feldman, 2007 and Gray et al., 2017.

claim: Current clinical and scientific tools used for evaluating distractibility and inattention are greatly removed from the real-life experience in organic classrooms.
source: However, current clinical and scientific tools used for evaluating and quantifying the constructs of 'distractibility' and 'inattention' are greatly removed from the real-life experience in organic classrooms and other ecological contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the discussion of limitations of current tools.

claim: Current tools for evaluating attention lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity to reliably capture real-life attention challenges.
source: Unfortunately, in recent years, there is a growing understanding that these tools lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity to reliably capture the type and severity of real-life attention challenges that people face outside the lab or the clinic (Rabiner et al., 2010; Narad et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2018; Mulraney et al., 2022; Hobbiss and Lavie, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research on limitations of attention assessment tools.

claim: Recent years have seen increased use of virtual reality (VR) in cognitive research.
source: In attempt to create laboratory-based tasks that are more ecologically valid, and better capture the type of attentional challenges faced in real-life, recent years have seen increased use of virtual reality (VR) in cognitive research (Parsons, 2015; Seesjärvi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parsons, 2015 and Seesjärvi et al., 2022.

claim: CPT tasks administered in VR classroom environments show greater sensitivity for AD(H)D classification relative to standard evaluations.
source: For example, it has been suggested that CPT tasks administered in VR classroom environments show greater sensitivity for AD(H)D classification relative to standard evaluations and can provide more refined measures of attention and distractibility (Rizzo et al., 2006; Neguț et al., 2017; Coleman et al., 2019; Parsons et al., 2019; Stokes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous VR classroom studies.

claim: Most VR classroom studies use relatively non-ecological tasks and rely primarily on indirect behavioral outcomes.
source: However, to date, most VR classroom studies still use relatively non-ecological tasks, and rely primarily on indirect behavioral outcomes to assess aspects of attentional performance.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the review of existing VR classroom literature.

claim: Neural speech tracking captures aspects of sensory and linguistic processing of speech.
source: Neural speech tracking of the teacher's lesson, which captures aspects of its sensory and linguistic processing, and is known to be reduced under conditions of inattention or distraction (Ding and Simon, 2012a; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Huang and Elhilali, 2020; Holtze et al., 2021; Kaufman and Zion‐Golumbic, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural speech tracking.

claim: Neural speech tracking is reduced under conditions of inattention or distraction.
source: Neural speech tracking of the teacher's lesson, which captures aspects of its sensory and linguistic processing, and is known to be reduced under conditions of inattention or distraction (Ding and Simon, 2012a; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Huang and Elhilali, 2020; Holtze et al., 2021; Kaufman and Zion‐Golumbic, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural speech tracking.

claim: Neural event-related potentials reflect exogenous capture of attention by salient irrelevant stimuli.
source: Neural event-related potentials (ERPs), transient changes in SC, and overt gaze-shifts following unexpected sound-events in the background of the classroom. These metrics are thought to reflect exogenous capture of attention, increases in arousal and potentially distraction by salient irrelevant stimuli (Posner, 1980; Bidet-Caulet et al., 2015; Masson and Bidet-Caulet, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on attention capture.

claim: Gaze-shifts away from the teacher are associated with attention-shifts and distractibility.
source: The frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and time spent looking around the classroom, metrics associated with attention-shifts and distractibility (Grosbras et al., 2005; Schomaker et al., 2017), and are often heightened in individuals with AD(H)D (Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022; Selaskowski et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on gaze patterns and attention.

claim: Gaze-shifts away from the teacher are often heightened in individuals with AD(H)D.
source: The frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and time spent looking around the classroom, metrics associated with attention-shifts and distractibility (Grosbras et al., 2005; Schomaker et al., 2017), and are often heightened in individuals with AD(H)D (Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022; Selaskowski et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ADHD and gaze patterns.

claim: The power of alpha- and beta-oscillations is often associated with increased mind-wandering or boredom.
source: The power of alpha- and beta-oscillations, which are often associated with increased mind-wandering or boredom (Clarke et al., 2001; Boudewyn and Carter, 2018; Jin et al., 2019), and some have suggested may be altered in individuals with AD(H)D (although use of spectral signatures as biomarkers for AD(H)D is highly controversial; Gloss et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on oscillatory activity and attention.

claim: Use of spectral signatures as biomarkers for AD(H)D is highly controversial.
source: The power of alpha- and beta-oscillations, which are often associated with increased mind-wandering or boredom (Clarke et al., 2001; Boudewyn and Carter, 2018; Jin et al., 2019), and some have suggested may be altered in individuals with AD(H)D (although use of spectral signatures as biomarkers for AD(H)D is highly controversial; Gloss et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gloss et al., 2016.

claim: Participants demonstrated overall good performance on the comprehension task, achieving an average accuracy of 87.87%.
source: Participants demonstrated overall good performance on the comprehension task, achieving an average accuracy of 87.87% (±6.77% SEM).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the behavioral analysis.

claim: Performance levels were similarly good in both the Events and Quiet conditions.
source: Performance levels were similarly good in both the Events and Quiet conditions, indicating that the presence of occasional sound-events did not disrupt overall understanding of the mini-lessons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing performance across conditions.

claim: The presence of occasional sound-events did not disrupt overall understanding of the mini-lessons.
source: Performance levels were similarly good in both the Events and Quiet conditions, indicating that the presence of occasional sound-events did not disrupt overall understanding of the mini-lessons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing similar performance across conditions.

claim: No significant differences in performance were found between groups in either condition.
source: No significant differences in performance were found between groups, in either condition [Events: t(47) = 1.052, p = 0.297, Cohen's d = 0.30, Bayes Factor (BF10) = 0.448 (weak support of H0); Quiet: t(47) = 1.004, p = 0.320, Cohen's d = 0.28, BF10 = 0.430 (weak support for H0); Figure 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups.
source: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups showing the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2), and the model's predictive power following the traditional mid-central topography associated with auditory responses (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRF analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRFs showed the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2).
source: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups showing the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2), and the model's predictive power following the traditional mid-central topography associated with auditory responses (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRF analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No significant between-group differences were found in the predictive power of the encoding model.
source: No significant between-group differences were found in the predictive power of the encoding model (averaged across electrodes), and Bayes analysis indicates moderate support for the null hypothesis [t(47) = 0.23, p = 0.814, Cohen's d = 0.067, BF10 = 0.15].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the encoding model data.

claim: The AD(H)D group showed slightly lower reconstruction correlations for the teacher's speech in the decoding model.
source: However, when using a decoding model, which considers all electrodes in one model, we did find slightly lower reconstruction correlations for the teacher's speech in the AD(H)D group relative to controls [t(47) = –1.948, p = 0.057, Cohen's d = –0.557, BF10 = 1.308 (weak/moderate support for H1); Figure 2C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the decoding model data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Participants spent most of the time looking at the teacher (60.2 ± 20.9% SEM of each trial).
source: Analysis of gaze-patterns showed that, as expected, participants spent most of the time looking at the teacher (60.2 ± 20.9% SEM of each trial).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: There is large variability across participants in the amount of time spent looking at the teacher.
source: However, we also note the large variability across participants, with some focusing almost exclusively on the teacher (near 100%) and others spending less than 40% of the trial looking at the teacher.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis showing variability.

claim: No significant differences were found between groups in the amount of time spent looking at the teacher.
source: No significant differences were found, however BF analysis indicated that the null hypotheses was not strongly supported [Percent gaze-time at teacher: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.899, p = 0.372, Cohen's d = –0.257, BF10 = 0.397 (weak support for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.597, p = 0.553, Cohen's d = –0.170, BF10 = 0.33 (weak support for H0); Number of gaze-shifts away from teacher: Events Condition: t(47) = 1.265, p = 0.211, Cohen's d = 0.361, BF10 = 0.547 (weak support for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = 0.644, p = 0.522, Cohen's d = 0.184, BF10 = 0.338 (weak support for H0); Figure 3C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neural ERPs showed three prominent centro-parietal components: a negative peak around 100 ms (N1), followed by two positive peaks around 240 and 350 ms (P2 and P3).
source: Visual inspection of the neural ERPs showed three prominent centro-parietal components – a negative peak around 100 ms, which corresponds to the early sensory N1; followed by two positive peaks around 240 and 350 ms, which likely corresponds to the P2 and P3 responses, respectively (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The early N1 response was significantly larger in the AD(H)D group.
source: Statistical analysis comparing ERPs in the AD(H)D vs. Control groups (collapsed across both Event-types) showed that the early N1 response was significantly larger in the AD(H)D group (p < 0.05, cluster correction; Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: No significant differences between groups were found for the later P2 response.
source: However, no significant differences between groups were found for the later P2 response.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data.

claim: Both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type.
source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The N1 was larger for Artificial sounds compared to non-verbal human sounds.
source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The P2 was larger for non-verbal human sounds compared to Artificial sounds.
source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sound-events elicited clear event-related changes in the phasic SC response, which peaked 2–3 s after the sounds.
source: Sound-events elicited clear event-related changes in the phasic SC response, which peaked 2–3 s after the sounds, and took another ~1 s to return to baseline (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin conductance data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The event-related SC response is consistent with the well-documented orienting reflex.
source: This response is consistent with the well-documented orienting reflex, elicited following salient events.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the orienting reflex and inference from the observed SC response pattern.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Event-type on event-related SC, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds.
source: A mixed ANOVA showed a significant main effects of Event-type, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds [F(1, 47) = 7.88, p = 0.007, η2 = 0.143], however there was no significant main effect of Group [F(1, 47) = 0.4, p = 0.53, η2 = 0.008] or interaction between them [F(1, 47) = 0.02, p = 0.87, η2 = 0.0005; Figure 5B, C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no significant main effect of Group on event-related SC.
source: A mixed ANOVA showed a significant main effects of Event-type, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds [F(1, 47) = 7.88, p = 0.007, η2 = 0.143], however there was no significant main effect of Group [F(1, 47) = 0.4, p = 0.53, η2 = 0.008] or interaction between them [F(1, 47) = 0.02, p = 0.87, η2 = 0.0005; Figure 5B, C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sound-events did not elicit more frequent overt gaze-shifts away from the teacher relative to control epochs.
source: However, no significant differences were found, suggesting that the sound-events did not elicit more frequent overt gaze-shifts away from the teacher, relative to what might be observed when no sound-events are present [t(48) = 1.34, p = 0.18; Figure 6A].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The likelihood of performing event-related gaze-shifts was not different for the two Event-types or in the two Groups.
source: We also tested whether the likelihood of performing event-related gaze-shifts was different for the two Event-types (Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds) or in the two Groups (AD(H)D vs. Control) but did not find any significant main effects or interactions [Group: F(47) = 0.18, p = 0.67, η2 = 0.003; Condition: F(47) = 2.25, p = 0.14, η2 = 0.045; Interaction: F(47) = 0.51, p = 0.47, η2 = 0.01; Figure 6B].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No significant differences between groups were found in alpha-power in either the Events or Quiet condition.
source: However, none of the comparisons revealed any significant differences between groups, in either frequency band (Figure 7C) [Alpha-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.656, p = 0.514, Cohen's d = –0.18, BF10=0.34 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.394, p = 0.695, Cohen's d = –0.11, BF10 = 0.30 (moderate evidence for H0); Beta-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –1.01, p = 0.315, Cohen's d = –0.29, BF10 = 0.43 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.484, p = 0.630, Cohen's d = –0.14, BF10 = 0.314 (moderate evidence for H0)].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spectral EEG data shown in Figure 7.

claim: No significant differences between groups were found in beta-power in either the Events or Quiet condition.
source: However, none of the comparisons revealed any significant differences between groups, in either frequency band (Figure 7C) [Alpha-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.656, p = 0.514, Cohen's d = –0.18, BF10=0.34 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.394, p = 0.695, Cohen's d = –0.11, BF10 = 0.30 (moderate evidence for H0); Beta-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –1.01, p = 0.315, Cohen's d = –0.29, BF10 = 0.43 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.484, p = 0.630, Cohen's d = –0.14, BF10 = 0.314 (moderate evidence for H0)].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spectral EEG data shown in Figure 7.

claim: No significant differences between the two Groups were observed for the global tonic or phasic SC metrics in either condition.
source: No significant differences between the two Groups were observed for the global tonic or phasic SC metrics, in either the Events or Quiet condition [Phasic SC (Figure 7D, E): Events Condition: t(47) = –0.003, p = 0.99, Cohen's d = –0.0009, BF10 = 0.285 (moderate evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.51, p = 0.61, Cohen's d = –0.146, BF10 = 0.317 (moderate evidence for H0); Tonic SC: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.85, p = 0.398, Cohen's d = –0.244, BF10 = 0.383 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –1.65, p = 0.104, Cohen's d = –0.476, BF10 = 0.865 (weak evidence for H0)].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 7.

claim: None of the pairwise correlations between neurophysiological measures were significant after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: None of the correlations were significant after correcting for multiple comparisons (fdr-correction), however three pairs did reach significance before correction (Speech-Decoding vs. ERP-P2: r = –0.33, p = 0.021; TRF-N1 vs. event-related SC: r = –0.3, p = 0.033; ERP-N1 vs. event-related SC: r = 0.29, p = 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neurophysiological measures.

claim: The omnibus logistic regression model containing all 10 measures achieved χ2 = 15.6 with an AUC of 0.807 for predicting group allocation.
source: An 'omnibus' model containing all 10 measures achieved χ2 = 15.6 with an AUC of 0.807 for predicting group allocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate logistic regression analysis.

claim: The two most dominant measures in predicting group allocation were the ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding.
source: We assessed the relative contribution (dominance) of each measure by comparing the AUC of the omnibus model to 10 models with a single measure held-out. Table 1 shows ΔAUC contributed by each measure, indicating that the two most dominant measures were the ERP-N1 (positive contribution) and Speech Decoding (negative contribution), which were also the only two measures whose addition to the model reduced the AIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by dominance analysis of the logistic regression model shown in Table 1.

claim: ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding together contributed an AUC of 0.15 to the omnibus model.
source: Together, these two measures contributed an AUC of 0.15 to the omnibus model, which corresponds to half of the model's fit (Δχ2 = 11.8, p = 0.003 relative to a model with both measures held-out).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate regression analysis.

claim: The omnibus linear regression model containing all 10 measures achieved F(10, 38) = 1.48 (p = 0.18) with an R2 of 0.28 for predicting ASRS scores.
source: An 'omnibus' model containing all 10 achieved F(10, 38) = 1.48 (p = 0.18) with an R2 of 0.28 for predicting ASRS scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear regression analysis.

claim: The most dominant measures for predicting ASRS scores were ERP-N1, Gaze-shifts, Alpha-power, and ERP-P2.
source: The most dominant measures, who contributed at least ΔR2 > 0.3 the model, were the ERP-N1 (β = 0.3), Gaze-shifts (β = 0.288), Alpha-power (β = 0.2) and ERP-P2 (β = –0.182).
evidence: This claim is supported by dominance analysis of the linear regression model shown in Table 2.

claim: A multivariate regression model containing only the four most dominant measures significantly predicted ASRS scores (R2 = 0.227, p = 0.021).
source: Although the omnibus model was not significant (see above), a multivariate regression model that contained only the four most dominant measures did significantly predicted ASRS scores (R2 = 0.227, p = 0.021), and collectively contributed ΔR2 = 0.225 (p = 0.032) to the omnibus model.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear regression analysis.

claim: Enhanced N1 responses are often associated with heightened sensory sensitivity.
source: Enhanced N1 responses are often associated with heightened sensory sensitivity (Heil, 1997; Lütkenhöner and Klein, 2007), perceptual predictability (Chennu et al., 2013; Lange, 2013; Schwartze and Kotz, 2015), and may reflect a transient detector mechanism of surprising events that can potentially (though not necessarily) trigger an attention shift (Näätänen and Picton, 1987; Escera et al., 1998; Escera et al., 2003; Berti, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on N1 responses.

claim: Most studies comparing auditory ERPs in individuals with and without AD(H)D using traditional paradigms have not reported differences in early-sensory components such as the N1.
source: Interestingly, most studies comparing auditory ERPs in individuals with and without AD(H)D, using more traditional paradigms (e.g., oddball), typically have not reported differences in early-sensory components such as the N1, but rather sometimes find group differences for later ERP responses (Barry et al., 2003; Gumenyuk et al., 2005; Kaiser et al., 2020; Peisch et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous ERP studies in ADHD.

claim: The discrepancy in N1 findings between this study and traditional paradigms is attributed to the non-ecological nature of most traditional paradigms.
source: As discussed below, we attribute these discrepancies to the non-ecological nature of most traditional paradigm.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors to explain the discrepancy in findings.

claim: Neural speech tracking of continuous speech is known to be modulated by attention.
source: Neural speech tracking of continuous speech is known to be modulated by attention, and is reduced when speech is not attended (Ding and Simon, 2012b; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Petersen et al., 2017; Vanthornhout et al., 2019; Kaufman and Zion‐Golumbic, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural speech tracking.

claim: The magnitude of the N1 to sound-events and speech tracking of the teacher were not correlated with each other.
source: Interestingly, since the magnitude of the N1 to sound-events and speech tracking of the teacher were not correlated with each other, these results do not support the notion of an inherent 'tradeoff' between paying attention to the teacher and responding to irrelevant stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between these measures.

claim: The two groups (ADHD and Control) are clearly separable based on ASRS scores but are far from uniform in the severity of symptoms experienced.
source: This is evident from inspecting the distribution of ASRS scores in the current sample, which shows that although the two groups are clearly separable from each other, they are far from uniform in the severity of symptoms experienced.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the ASRS score distribution data.

claim: Higher alpha-power is associated with reduced levels of attention/arousal.
source: Higher alpha-power is associated with reduced levels of attention/arousal, and is consistently found to increase in conditions of boredom, tiredness or prolonged time on tasks (Clarke et al., 2001; Dockree et al., 2007; Palva and Palva, 2007; Wöstmann et al., 2017; Boudewyn and Carter, 2018; Jin et al., 2019; Haro et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on alpha oscillations.

claim: Several studies have found higher baseline alpha-power in individuals with AD(H)D versus controls.
source: Several studies have also found higher baseline alpha-power in individuals with AD(H)D versus controls (Barry et al., 2003; Johnstone et al., 2013; Bozhilova et al., 2022; Michelini et al., 2022), although results are not always consistent (Loo and Makeig, 2012; Johnstone et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on alpha power in ADHD.

claim: Gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions.
source: Similarly, gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions (Marius 't Hart et al., 2009; Foulsham et al., 2011; Risko and Kingstone, 2011; Risko et al., 2012; Hoppe et al., 2018), and recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D (Braga et al., 2016; Türkan et al., 2016; Vakil et al., 2019; Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on gaze patterns and attention.

claim: Recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D.
source: Similarly, gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions (Marius 't Hart et al., 2009; Foulsham et al., 2011; Risko and Kingstone, 2011; Risko et al., 2012; Hoppe et al., 2018), and recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D (Braga et al., 2016; Türkan et al., 2016; Vakil et al., 2019; Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on gaze patterns in ADHD.

claim: Individuals who exhibited higher alpha-power, performed more frequent gaze-shifts and had larger N1 response to background sound-events were more likely to report experiencing attentional difficulties in real life.
source: The current results extend these findings to more ecological contexts and indicate that individuals who exhibited higher alpha-power, performed more frequent gaze-shifts and had larger N1 response to background sound-events in our VR classroom were more likely to report experiencing attentional difficulties in real life.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate regression analysis showing these measures predict ASRS scores.

claim: No single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining differences between individuals in attentional functioning.
source: What is clear, though, is that no single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining differences between the individuals – whether through the lens of clinical diagnosis or through report of symptoms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the multivariate analysis results showing multiple measures contribute to explaining variance.

claim: Attentional challenges may manifest in a variety of different ways, indexed through different neurophysiological responses.
source: These data emphasize the complex nature of attentional functioning, especially under realistic conditions, and that fact that 'attentional challenges' may manifest in a variety of different ways, indexed though different neurophysiological responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that multiple uncorrelated measures contribute to explaining ADHD symptoms.

claim: The P3a ERP component is typically observed at a latency of ~250–400 ms after hearing novel or surprising sounds.
source: In traditional ERP studies, distractibility by irrelevant stimuli is often associated with a family of late-latency positive neural responses (the P300 family), and specifically the P3a ERP component, which is typically observed at a latency of ~250–400 ms after hearing novel or surprising sounds (SanMiguel et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2013; Masson and Bidet-Caulet, 2019; Barry et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the P3a component.

claim: Past studies have shown reduced P3a responses in individuals with AD(H)D.
source: Moreover, past studies have shown reduced P3a responses in individuals with AD(H)D (Barry et al., 2003; Gumenyuk et al., 2005; Kaiser et al., 2020; Peisch et al., 2021; Kwasa et al., 2023), leading us to expect a similar pattern here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on P3a in ADHD.

claim: The P3a is typically observed in tasks that require high levels of perceptual vigilance to discriminate between specific stimulus features.
source: The P3a is typically observed in tasks that require high levels of perceptual vigilance to discriminate between specific stimulus features, such as the pitch, duration or intensity of sounds presented in an oddball paradigm.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of P3a research and the typical experimental contexts in which it is observed.

claim: In oddball paradigms, 'distractor' sounds are within the focus of participants' endogenous attention rather than truly 'background' stimuli.
source: Accordingly, although these 'distractor' stimuli do not require an explicit response, they are in fact within the focus of participants' endogenous attention, rather than truly 'background' stimuli (Makov et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the nature of attention in oddball paradigms, supported by a citation.

claim: The role of novel sound-events in the VR classroom differs substantially from their role in oddball paradigms.
source: This differs substantially from the role of the novel sounds-events in the VR classroom task used here, where sound-events are clearly in the background– both spatially and semantically – and occur in parallel to an ongoing speech stimulus (the lecture) that participants are primarily paying attention to.
evidence: This claim is based on inference comparing the current experimental design to traditional oddball paradigms.

claim: Participants in both groups achieved similar behavioral performance in the Quiet and Events condition.
source: Participants in both groups achieved similar behavioral performance in the Quiet and Events condition, suggesting that the presence of occasional sound-events ultimately did not ultimately impair their ability to understand the content of the mini-lectures (at least at the level probed by our comprehension questions).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: The task was deliberately chosen to mimic the level of information processing required in real-life learning contexts.
source: These results should be interpreted bearing in mind the details of the current task design – we deliberately chose a task that would mimic the level of information processing required in real-life learning contexts as opposed to speeded-response tasks used in traditional attention research that encourage failures of performance by creating perceptually 'extreme' conditions (Hall et al., 2016; Barkley, 2019; Arrondo et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design choices made by the authors.

claim: Neurophysiological indications of somewhat reduced attention do not necessarily translate to poorer behavioral outcomes.
source: Under these conditions, individuals with and without AD(H)D were able to maintain good performance despite the occasional acoustic disturbances (Mandal et al., 2024), indicating that neurophysiological indication of somewhat reduced attention do not necessarily translate to poorer behavioral outcomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that neural differences were observed without corresponding behavioral differences.

claim: The SC orienting reflex is considered obligatory and automatic.
source: This response is considered obligatory and automatic, and does not require allocation of attention as it can be observed during sleep and other unconscious states (albeit the magnitude of these responses can vary as a function of attention).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the orienting reflex.

claim: There has been much debate regarding the relationship between the SC orienting reflex and early neural responses.
source: Indeed, there has been much debate regarding the relationship between the SC orienting reflex and early neural responses, with conflicting results reported across studies (Lim et al., 1996; MacDonald and Barry, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results.

claim: Peripheral auditory stimuli may be less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention.
source: These results might indicate that peripheral auditory stimuli are, generally, less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention (Turoman and Vergauwe, 2024; Mandal et al., 2024), or that in ecological audiovisual settings individuals are less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the null finding for gaze-shifts, supported by citations.

claim: In ecological audiovisual settings individuals may be less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
source: These results might indicate that peripheral auditory stimuli are, generally, less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention (Turoman and Vergauwe, 2024; Mandal et al., 2024), or that in ecological audiovisual settings individuals are less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the null finding for gaze-shifts.

claim: Classification of the AD(H)D group was based on their prior clinical diagnosis.
source: First, as noted, classification of the AD(H)D group was based on their prior clinical diagnosis, which likely varied across participants in terms of diagnosis approach and age of diagnosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: The two groups were distinguishable in their self-reported ASRS scores.
source: Although the two groups were distinguishable in their self-reported ASRS scores, a more reliable assessment of the severity of current AD(H)D symptoms might have been achieved if we had conducted a full clinical assessment of all participants, as per the acceptable clinical guidelines (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ASRS data showing significant group differences.

claim: This study was conducted on adults, whereas the majority of AD(H)D research has focused on children.
source: Second, this study was conducted on adults, whereas the majority of AD(H)D research – and particularly all VR classroom studies – have focused on children (Pollak et al., 2009; Neguț et al., 2017; Schweitzer and Rizzo, 2022; Seesjärvi et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the sample characteristics and comparison to previous research.

claim: The adult cohort tested included primarily university students with relatively high cognitive and learning abilities.
source: Moreover, the adult cohort tested here included primarily university students, who do not represent all adults but rather are a subgroup with relatively high cognitive and learning abilities, who are accustomed to sitting in lectures for long periods of time (Henrich et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the sample characteristics and potential limitations.

claim: The lack of group differences in some metrics may be because these individuals have learned to deal with distraction and have developed appropriate strategies.
source: Hence, it is possible that the lack of group differences in some metrics in the current dataset (and particularly in their behavioral outcomes) is because these individuals have learned to deal with distraction and have developed appropriate strategies, which allow them to thrive in academic settings.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about why certain null results were observed.

claim: Withstanding distraction in real-life contexts may be improved through training and good habit-forming, even in individuals with AD(H)D.
source: Specifically, they suggest that withstanding distraction in real-life contexts may be improved through training and good habit-forming, even in individuals with AD(H)D.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the results.

claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds.
source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from ERP analysis.

claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit reduced speech tracking of the teacher.
source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from speech tracking analysis.

claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher.
source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate analysis showing gaze-shifts predict ASRS scores.

claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit somewhat increased alpha-power.
source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate analysis showing alpha-power predicts ASRS scores.

claim: The neurophysiological metrics measured were not correlated with each other.
source: Interestingly, since these metrics were not correlated with each other, they likely represent different ways through which inattention or distraction may manifest, rather than a general 'biomarker' of inattention.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing weak correlations between measures.

claim: The neurophysiological metrics likely represent different ways through which inattention or distraction may manifest.
source: Interestingly, since these metrics were not correlated with each other, they likely represent different ways through which inattention or distraction may manifest, rather than a general 'biomarker' of inattention.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between measures.

claim: AD(H)D may not be characterized by a specific 'neural marker' indicating attentional deficits, particularly when tested under ecological circumstances.
source: Counter to some prevalent notions, these data suggest that AD(H)D may not be characterized by a specific 'neural marker' indicating attentional deficits, particularly when tested under ecological circumstances (Barkley, 2019; Faraone et al., 2021; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the results and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There is a need to adopt more nuanced and dimensional approaches to defining attention-disorders.
source: Rather, they resonate with recent calls to revisit the parameters used for defining 'attention-disorders' and the need to adopt more nuanced and dimensional approach, as well as designing more ecologically valid means of testing, in order to better characterize and understand the complex nature of real-life attentional challenges (Marcus and Barry, 2011; Heidbreder, 2015; Morris et al., 2022; Elahi et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature calling for changes in ADHD research approaches.

claim: Fifty-four participants initially participated in the study.
source: Fifty-four participants initially participated in the study; however, the data from five participants were excluded due to technical issues or their voluntary request to discontinue participation.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size and data collection.

claim: The final sample consisted of 49 participants (21 male, 28 female; 46 right-handed, 3 left-handed).
source: The final sample consisted of 49 participants (21 male, 28 female; 46 right-handed, 3 left-handed).
evidence: This is a statement about the final sample characteristics.

claim: Of the 49 participants, 24 had a prior clinical diagnosis of AD(H)D, and 25 did not.
source: Of these participants, 24 had a prior clinical diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (AD(H)D group), and 25 participants did not (control group).
evidence: This is a statement about the group composition.

claim: The two groups were matched for age, which ranged between 20 and 38 years.
source: The two groups were matched for age, which ranged between 20 and 38 years (mean age of all participants: 26.9 ± 3.0; AD(H)D participants: 26.7 ± 3.7; control participants: 25.7 ± 4.4).
evidence: This is a statement about the sample matching procedure.

claim: The majority of participants were university students.
source: The majority of participants were university students.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample characteristics.

claim: The experiment was scheduled at least 12 hr after the last dose of medication for participants in the AD(H)D group.
source: Participants in the AD(H)D group were questioned about their medication intake regimen, and the experiment was scheduled at least 12 hr after their last dose of medication.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: The ASRS questionnaire has been shown to have good psychometric properties and high sensitivity for AD(H)D diagnosis.
source: All participants completed a self-report questionnaire assessing AD(H)D symptoms (ASRS-v1.1; Adler et al., 2006, Hebrew version: Zohar and Konfortes, 2010), which has been shown to have good psychometric properties high sensitivity for AD(H)D diagnosis (Kessler et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous validation studies of the ASRS.

claim: The group diagnosed with AD(H)D exhibited significantly higher ASRS scores compared to the control group.
source: As expected, the group diagnosed with AD(H)D exhibited significantly higher ASRS scores compared to the control group [t(47) = 8.49, p < 0.001; see Figure 9].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ASRS data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The VR classroom platform was developed using the Unity game engine.
source: The VR classroom platform was developed using the Unity game engine (unity.com; JavaScript and C# programming).
evidence: This is a statement about the technical development of the VR platform.

claim: The experiment consisted of 30 trials.
source: The experiment consisted of 30 trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Most trials (22) contained occasional background event-sounds (Events condition).
source: Most trials (22) contained occasional background event-sound (Events condition; with 5 of both types sound-events per trial, separated by 3–7 s; Figure 10B), whereas 8 trials did not, serving as a Quiet baseline condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design shown in Figure 10.

claim: Eight trials did not contain event-sounds, serving as a Quiet baseline condition.
source: Most trials (22) contained occasional background event-sound (Events condition; with 5 of both types sound-events per trial, separated by 3–7 s; Figure 10B), whereas 8 trials did not, serving as a Quiet baseline condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: In total, 104 sound-events were presented throughout the experiment (52 of each type).
source: In total, 104 sound-events were presented throughout the experiment (52 of each type).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: Neural activity was recorded using 64 active ag-agCl EEG electrodes and was sampled at 1024 Hz.
source: Neural activity was recorded using 64 active ag-agCl EEG electrodes (BioSemi) and was sampled at 1024 Hz.
evidence: This is a statement about the data acquisition methods.

claim: Speech-tracking analysis could only be performed reliably in the Events condition.
source: As noted in the methods section, speech-tracking analysis could only be performed reliably in the Events condition, and we used a multivariate approach to account for variance in the neural activity due to the presence of event-sounds (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for comparison with univariate analysis).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological constraints of the analysis.

claim: The multivariate model was able to explain a larger degree of the variance in the neural response compared to the univariate model.
source: When comparing the predictive power of the univariate and multivariate models, both models yielded significant predictive power relative to null-permutations, however the multivariate model was able to explain a larger degree of the variance in the neural response [t(48) = 10.354, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.268, Bayes Factor (BF10) = +100 (Extreme evidence for H1)].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model performance shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
